summary: Registers four MIME types for the parity-based forward error correction format used with RTP: audio, video, text, and application versions of parityfec. These labels let applications recognize streams that carry extra repair data. It was replaced by RFC 5109.

eli5.summary: When sending a video, you can add a few spare pieces so lost ones can be rebuilt. This gives name tags to those spare-piece streams. A newer document later replaced it.

subtitle: Names for forward error correction streams in RTP

tldr.problem: RTP streams that carry parity-based forward error correction data need standardized MIME type labels so applications can recognize and handle them correctly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3009 registers four MIME types (audio/parityfec, video/parityfec, text/parityfec, application/parityfec) that identify FEC streams for different media types when carried in RTP.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use these MIME labels to signal and negotiate FEC streams in RTP sessions, improving error resilience. RFC 5109 later superseded it with an improved format.

today: RFC 3009 was replaced by RFC 5109, which defines an improved RTP payload format for forward error correction that provides better performance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 2733 defines a generic RTP payload format for forward error correction (FEC) that uses traditional parity-based channel codes. This technique allows RTP participants to improve loss resiliency by computing and sending additional repair data alongside the original media. To support this, four new MIME types are needed to identify FEC streams: audio/parityfec, video/parityfec, text/parityfec, and application/parityfec. This RFC registers those types following IETF procedures.
sections.eli5: Some RTP messages include extra repair data to help rebuild lost pieces. These registrations give those streams official names.

sections.title: MIME Type Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers four MIME types, one for each media class. Each registration follows the same pattern and references RFC 2733 for the actual format specification.

Key points across all registrations: the FEC data has no required parameters, as the FEC frame rate matches the original media's rate. The encoding is only defined for RTP transport. Security considerations reference RFC 2733. All four types are intended for common use in streaming applications that need loss recovery.
sections.eli5: Four official names are registered, one each for audio, video, text, and application repair data streams. They all follow the same rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This MIME registration itself does not introduce additional security considerations beyond those in RFC 2733, which defines the actual FEC payload format. Security properties of FEC streams depend on the underlying media protection and the RTP security mechanisms in use.
sections.eli5: The registration doesn't add any new security problems. Any security issues would come from the original protection method used by the repair data.

sections.title: Key References
sections.content: RFC 2733 defines the RTP payload format for generic forward error correction that these MIME types support. RFC 2048 specifies the general MIME type registration procedures. RFC 2327 describes the Session Description Protocol (SDP) which uses MIME types to negotiate media parameters.
sections.eli5: Other documents explain what FEC is, how to register MIME types officially, and how RTP sessions decide what formats to use.
